Getting the garden ready

Florence, 12th July. In the garden behind the trattoria, under Aldo's wisteria, the party for Pietro's eleventh birthday is being prepared. Viola, nearly fourteen months old, is toddling among the tables.
The older I get, the more I like garden parties.
And the more Viola grows, the more she looks like Matei. Look how she frowns when she concentrates.
Looks like me? She's getting more and more Neapolitan! She shouts more and more.
And Pietro is getting taller and taller. Soon he'll be taller than you, Matei.
That's not hard. Graziella, is the cake bigger than last year's?
Much bigger than you think. I've invited more people than will fit in the garden.
Thank goodness Davide is here to help us. He's the kindest boy I've ever met.
And the quietest. The better I know him, the less he talks.
But the more he draws, the better he draws. Bellini says he's making progress faster than expected.
That's enough chatter, you two! The more we talk, the less we work. And the guests arrive at seven.
All right, all right. I'll take the chairs out as fast as I can.
And I'll take Viola out. All the more so since she's trying to eat a wisteria flower.

1. Più… più, meno… meno: the more… the more
To say that two things grow (or shrink) together, Italian uses "più… più" or "meno… meno", without articles (English uses "the more… the more"):
Più Viola cresce, più somiglia a Matei.
Più invecchio, più mi piacciono le feste.
The older I get, the more I like parties.
Più parliamo, meno lavoriamo.
Meno dormo, meno lavoro bene.
The less I sleep, the worse I work.
Don't translate word for word: NOT "Il più… il più" (as in English "the more"). Just say: "Più… più".
2. Sempre più, sempre meno: more and more
Viola shouts more and more.
I have less and less time.
With a verb and no adjective you say "sempre DI più / sempre DI meno": "Lavora sempre di più."
3. Comparing with an expectation: più di quanto…
When you compare reality with what you thought or expected, use "di quanto + subjunctive", "di quello che + indicative" or "del previsto":
più di quanto + subjunctive
È più grande di quanto pensi.
It's bigger than you think.
più di quanto + subj. (past)
È stato più bello di quanto pensassi.
It was more beautiful than I thought.
più di quello che + indicative
Costa più di quello che pensavo.
It costs more than I thought.
più del previsto
Fa progressi più in fretta del previsto.
He's making progress faster than expected.
4. The superlative + subjunctive
After a relative superlative (il più…, il migliore, l’unico, il primo, l’ultimo) the relative clause usually takes the SUBJUNCTIVE:
It's the best cake I've ever eaten.
He's the only one who knows how to restore this painting.
In fast speech you'll also hear the indicative ("il più bello che ho mai visto"), but with the subjunctive it sounds much better.

La tacca di Pietro

By seven the garden was already full, and the lower the sun sank behind the rooftops, the more people arrived. There were Pietro's schoolfriends, the neighbours from via Maggio, Signor Franco in a straw hat, Marco and Sara with a spare cake "in case Grandma's isn't enough". Davide had arrived first, as always, with a roll of paper under his arm that he wouldn't show anyone.

Pietro was happier than he had ever been. He was eleven, he had a watch with a blue strap that he had worn for three summers, a friend who drew better than anyone and a job as guide at the most famous workshop in the Oltrarno. "It's the best birthday I've ever had," he told everyone, even though the party had only just begun.

On a small table, propped against a bottle, was Giulia's tablet, with two windows open: on one side Grandma Assunta, in Naples, with a paper hat on her head; on the other Doina and Ion, in Sibiu, with Lupu barking every time someone sang. "The more the years go by," Assunta told the screen, "the bigger this family gets. Soon we'll need a television bigger than Vesuvius." Ion raised a glass of pălincă to the camera, and half the garden replied "Noroc!".

Viola, meanwhile, was the centre of attention. She had been walking for three months now, and the more she walked, the faster she got. She went from one table to the next, from one guest to the next, and everyone wanted to pick her up. But Viola wouldn't let anyone pick her up. She would stop, look at the person with her big dark eyes, frown exactly like her father, and set off again.

There was one problem, though, which the family was talking about more and more: Viola still didn't speak. She was fourteen months old and hadn't said a single word. Not "mamma", not "papà", not "nonna". Rosaria, in Naples, was more worried than she wanted to admit. Doina, in Sibiu, said that Matei had spoken late too, and then had never stopped. Giulia pretended not to think about it, but she thought about it more and more.

At about eight Bellini arrived, in a jacket despite the heat, with a parcel for Pietro. Inside was an old book on the history of the Uffizi, with a dedication: "To Pietro, the youngest guide Florence has ever had. The more you learn, the more you'll see." Pietro read it twice, then clutched it to his chest as if it were a treasure.

Signor Franco had a present too: an old railway ticket from 1962, Florence–Rome, the first one he had ever stamped as a young stationmaster. "The older I get, the fewer things I need," he told Pietro. "But I've kept this one for sixty years, waiting for the right person. A guide has to know that every journey begins with a ticket." Pietro put it inside Bellini's book, with the care of someone keeping a relic.

Then it was Davide's turn. He unrolled his paper on the table, extremely shy, as everyone gathered round. It was a pencil drawing of the trattoria, with the wisteria, the door, the first-floor window, and standing in front of the door, the whole family: Graziella in her apron, Matei and Giulia hand in hand, Viola in someone's arms, Pietro with his watch, Bellini with his hands behind his back. And at the top, very small, almost transparent, two men none of them had ever known: one with a moustache and a brush, the other with a red bicycle.

Graziella raised a hand to her mouth. Bellini took off his glasses and cleaned them for a long time, longer than necessary. "How did you know what they looked like?" Matei asked quietly. Davide shrugged. "The professor showed me Ernesto's photograph. And Signora Graziella has a photo of Aldo in the kitchen. I thought they should be there too. It's the most important party of the year."

After the cake, Pietro made his wish out loud, which you should never do. "I want a notch," he said. "On the door of Viola's room. Like Dad's." Marco, who was drinking, nearly choked. Graziella looked at her son. Then she said: "Let's go. Right now. Before he grows taller than I can bear."

They all went up to the first floor, in single file, and crowded in front of the nursery door. On the door frame were Marco's notches, from 1978 to 1991, Viola's "still in the tummy" and Viola's new one at one year old. Marco took a pencil and a knife, and Pietro stood against the door frame, very straight, holding his breath to look taller. Marco made the notch. Then he looked at it and laughed.

Pietro's notch, at eleven, was at exactly the same height as Marco's at eleven, in 1988. Not one centimetre more, not one less. "The more I look at you," Marco told his son, his voice trembling, "the more you look like your grandfather Aldo." Pietro didn't understand why all the grown-ups had suddenly started crying.

It was then that it happened. Viola, in Giulia's arms, leaned towards the door frame, stretched her little hand towards all those notches, old and new, and said, in a clear voice that everyone heard: "Guadda!" Then, as if that weren't clear enough, she repeated it, louder: "Guadda!"

The silence lasted two seconds. Then Bellini began to laugh, a laugh nobody had ever heard from him, deep and uncontrollable, until he had to lean against the wall. "Look," he said, wiping his eyes. "Her first word is 'look'. My grandfather would have gone mad with joy. Now she only needs the second half of the rule." Matei took his daughter from Giulia's arms and lifted her into the air. "The second half," he said, laughing, "we'll teach her as late as possible."

Later, when the last guests had gone, Matei and Giulia stayed in the garden under the wisteria, with Viola asleep in their arms. "The more I think about it," said Giulia, "the more incredible it seems. A few years ago I was a Neapolitan restorer who didn't know how to tell you she liked you." "And I was a Romanian who didn't know how to ask you out for a coffee," Matei replied. They laughed softly. Above them, among the violet flowers, the first stars were coming out.
